subject: gnomeTinkerer
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: gnome tinkerer with a backpack of gadgets.
Style: whimsical low-poly mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a gnome tinkerer model with a backpack of gadgets, aiming for a moderately detailed build of around 250 parts and several textures while keeping the API usage safe and correct. I'm working out realistic proportions, starting with the gnome's overall height including the hat.

Mapping out skeleton joints...

For the neck, I'm figuring out whether to build it as its own chain or construct the head joint separately as a tip aimed along the end tangent, parented to the chest. I'll try a simple neck chain with one or two points and a names list that gives me a clean neck-to-head hierarchy.

For the chest, I want to grab the last joint of the spine chain to use as the parent, maybe just indexing into the joints array rather than relying on a "tip" property that could be null. I'm also weighing whether to skin the whole torso with a sweep over the spine chain for a smoothly rounded body shape.

Thinking through the radius profile, I'm planning an elliptical cross-section that varies along the spine -- narrower at the hips, widest at the belly, tapering again at the chest -- with the two radii mapped to sideways and front-back directions relative to the chain's orientation. The spine path itself curves slightly forward as it rises, and the torso will eventually get colored to look like a shirt.

Settling on the gnome's look now: a classic red hat, a blue tunic, a brown leather apron with brass goggles for a tinkerer vibe, dark boots, a white-grey beard, warm skin tone, and a rosy nose for character.

For the backpack, I'm loading it up with gadgets using the clockwork kit — a telescope, brass horn, gear train, pressure gauge, copper coil, and a glowing lantern with tools sticking out, giving it that inventor's pack feel while keeping the gear components simple and controlled.

I'll trim imports to only what's used so the typechecker doesn't flag unused locals. Now I'm planning the texture set: an eye decal SVG with iris and highlight for the head, plus a glowing lens texture for the goggles.

I'm also sketching more decorative pieces — gauge and gear textures for the backpack, a blueprint scroll with an unrolled plane sticking out of the pack, a gear-and-wrench emblem decal for the apron, and star/moon patches for the hat.

For the base, I'm planning a small round grass/stone disc with mushrooms, scattered gears, a toolbox, and a wooden crate, plus a glowing lantern texture and a labeled oil jar for extra detail. Now I'm thinking through the beard shape, likely a big lofted white beard.

For the beard, I'll sweep a tapering curve from the chin down to the tip using an ellipse profile that starts wide and narrows, plus small sphere puffs for a mustache and spike clumps or braid strands for texture. Then for the face, I'll use a flat-shaded sphere head with a prominent nose and pointed ears.

For the eyes, I'll use decals placed on the skull's surface via the surface/around/at helper, computing a hit point near the head center and accepting that `.at` may need a non-null assertion since it can return null.

I'm leaning toward decals for eye whites and irises (using an SVG texture) plus separate bushy brow shapes above them, while keeping the skull itself a low-poly flat-shaded sphere since decals project cleanly onto faceted surfaces. Now I'm sizing the nose as a big round sphere sitting on the face.

For the ears I'm sketching pointed outline shapes extruded with a bit of thickness, defining coordinate points that curve out from the head and come to a sharp tip near the top.

For the hat, I'm building a floppy, drooping cone shape with a curved sweep that bends backward from the base, and planning a joint chain to let the hat flop naturally off the head bone.

Defining hat lathe outline...

Total height comes to about 1.06m, which feels reasonable for a gnome figure. I'm adding a small gold bell at the hat's tip, plus thinking about decorative touches like a star patch and a checkered band around the hat base, possibly using a torus ring positioned near the head.

Writing torus geometry parameters...

For the hat, I'll use a flat start cap and pointed end cap for the cone sweep, with the brim lathe covering the base. For goggles, I'm thinking the classic gnome-tinkerer placement: up on the hat band rather than over the eyes, with brass rings and glowing lenses positioned on the front surface of the hat cone, using a surface hit calculation to position them correctly.

Writing stick geometry code...

I'm working through how the elevation-based surface query resolves hits on the hat axis, then thinking about how to build the apron over the belly curve -- a flat extrude would clash with the body's curvature, so I'm considering draping or sweeping a flat leather section along the torso path instead.

Maybe better to use the torso's sector system directly: on a vertical tube, 0 marks the back side and 180 the front, so I can define a sector spanning roughly 130-230 degrees for the apron color over a chosen t-range, letting it wrap the surface exactly rather than draping a flat strip. That avoids the floating-strip problem entirely since the clock angle is continuous around the vertical spine.

Still writing paint logic...

Now I'm thinking through the belt itself, using a loop around a point near the waist with a slight lift, and considering whether to sweep a circular or rectangular cross-section along it since the orientation of the belt's width versus thickness isn't obvious yet.

For the buckle, I'm planning to stick a small brass box onto the belt's front surface, sizing it thin along the normal direction and wider along the surface, then embedding it slightly so it looks attached rather than floating.

Now I'm sketching the belt accessories - a hammer, screwdriver, and pliers hanging from loops, attaching their rod-and-box geometry to hip points using skin-relative sticks. Then I'm working out the arm skeleton chain, placing shoulders, elbows, and wrists symmetrically with a slight A-pose spread to keep limbs separated in the rest position.

Writing hand and finger joint chains...

Still working out finger coordinates...

I'll use catmull interpolation through the three arm points for a smoother curve, keeping the span count the same. For detail, I'm considering adding a rolled cuff near the elbow and maybe a leather bracer with gauge texture on the left forearm as a fun accessory touch.

Still working out the orientation math -- since the forearm tilts downward rather than along a clean axis, figuring out which angle on the sweep surface corresponds to "outward/up" is tricky and depends on how the tube's normal convention behaves for a mostly-vertical tube.

Instead, I'll just use a nearest-point query: picking a point offset outward and slightly up from the forearm's midpoint, then finding the closest surface hit to anchor the gauge housing there. From that hit point I can build a small cylindrical housing and attach a circular gauge face plane oriented along the hit's outward normal, with a slight offset so it sits just above the surface and displays the gauge texture.

For orientation I'm using the hit's normal as the direction and defaulting the up vector to world +Y so gauge numerals stay upright. This is getting fairly involved, but I'll proceed carefully, planning out each section and writing conservative API calls so nothing breaks. Now I'm settling on a flat color palette, keeping each string short.

Moving to the legs: I'm positioning hip joints, knees, and ankles, computing limb segment lengths versus the actual distance so the knees bend slightly forward, and building the leg chains as point arrays that get swept into trouser geometry with a brownish-green color. I'm also adding foot and toe joints to extend the chain for boots.

Adding boot details...

Boots just need one capsule on the ankle joint, with ground contact at the chain tip. For the torso I'm building a spine chain from the hips using a curved path through three points up to the chest joint, and I'm shaping the tunic to flare at the hips with wider radii that narrow going up.

I'm checking how the round end caps extend beyond the path endpoints -- the top cap near the chest risks overlapping into the neck and head region, and the bottom cap at the hips would extend below where the legs attach, so I need to tune the radii and cap sizes to avoid those collisions.

Switching the top to a flat cap and keeping the bottom round gives a cleaner tunic hem around y=0.33, leaving a reasonable 0.26 length of visible leg below. That settles the overall vertical proportions: feet at 0, hem at 0.33, chest at 0.58, head at 0.74.

I'm adding a trim ring at the hem and a separate belt loop near the hip using the skin's loop function, then planning a sweeping spine chain with a radius profile to shape the torso.

Now I'm working out the neck and head joints—placing a short neck chain between chest and head, sweeping it thin since it'll be hidden by the beard, and positioning the head sphere's center and scale just above it.

I'll decide to keep everything in model coordinates rather than local bone axes, since that's simpler and more robust than tracking per-joint orientations. Then I move on to the jaw joint, parented under the head and aimed forward, planning a small mouth mostly concealed by the gnome's beard.

For the jaw itself I'm adding a small chin wedge in skin tone, hidden beneath the beard, plus a visible pink mouth slit between mustache and beard so there's some facial detail peeking through. I'm setting up the lower jaw as a skin-colored ellipsoid chin piece on the jaw bone, with a separate dark red mouth interior part on the head, and attaching the mustache to the head bone while the beard rides the jaw bone so it moves naturally with talking. I'm building the beard from several overlapping layered segments for a fuller look.

Writing beard chain geometry...

I'll combine the main beard sweep with two side spike clumps plus whisker cards for texture, then move on to crafting the mustache as two curved sweeps.

For the mustache, I'm using bezier curves to sweep outward from the nose on each side, adding a small dark red mouth ellipsoid beneath it, and placing a pink nose sphere above where the beard begins.

Now I'm positioning the nose slightly forward with a bulbous squashed shape, then placing the eyes symmetrically at an elevated angle relative to the head center, followed by curved white eyebrow tufts sweeping upward from above the eyes.

I realize the hat brim might overlap or shadow the eyes and brows, so I'm adjusting the head center and radius upward and recalculating the hat base and eye/brow positions to keep everything visible beneath the brim.

Working through the brim geometry now, making it wider than the head so it droops floppily while keeping ears clear underneath at their position.

For the cheeks I'll add small pink blush spheres embedded near the face, and use a low-poly flat-shaded sphere for the skull base. The ears get extruded with a slight thickness, oriented outward and back using a cross-product to figure out the right axes.

Now I'm designing the backpack as the main feature -- a boxy leather satchel shape with bevels positioned centered on the back, planning out its dimensions and placement before adding the straps.

For the straps, I'm sketching curved paths that drape from the pack top over each shoulder down to the front chest, then sweeping a thin flattened tube along those curves to form the strap geometry, while working out the right orientation for the strap's cross-section as it bends over the shoulder.

I'm draping strap points onto the nearest torso surface, with the pack attaching around the back near z -0.12, and setting up a dedicated "pack" bone under the chest/spine so the gear joints can animate independently. Now I'm sketching the main pack body as a rounded box shape.

Still writing pack details...

Now I'm sketching the gadget layout: a telescoping brass spyglass angled up on one side, a flared brass horn/trumpet on the other, and a little three-blade propeller mounted on a rod at the top center, possibly as a hinged "fan" joint for a playful spinning effect.

I'm also planning the back face with a cluster of brass gears and a gauge dial, a glowing orange lantern hanging from a hook on the lower side that sways on its own joint, a curling copper pipe connecting the tank to the horn, a spring coil accent, a rolled blueprint scroll tied to the top with a hanging textured page, and a scatter of tools tucked into the side of the pack.

Now I'm figuring out a copper boiler-style pressure tank lying across the pack with rivets, a gauge, and a valve wheel, plus a kettle or tin cup hanging beneath a flap underneath—keeping the whole thing to around 120 parts total. I'm working out the pack's exact position and depth so its front face just touches the torso's back without clipping, settling on a center z of -0.20 so the front sits at -0.125 and the back at -0.275, then starting to lay out the coordinates for each component beginning with the gear train on the back face.

Counting textures, I land on around eight: tuft, gauge, blueprint, emblem, hat star patch, label, lens, and mushroom spots, with one gear optionally getting its own tinted texture. Still tweaking gear math...
